lesson.child_mission: Rocks and soils have observable properties (hardness, grain size, colour, how they hold water) that help us describe and compare samples.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same science idea to a new object or material, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Compare sand and clay: two property differences and one way each affects plant watering.

FEEDBACK
Sand drains fast / gritty; clay holds water / sticky — plants in sand may need more frequent water; clay can stay wetter.

WATCH FOR
Calling all brown ground “dirt” without properties skips scientific description.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Test four soil/rock samples (touch, grain, water soak if allowed). Complete a property table and sort samples with a written rule.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Rocks and soils have observable properties (hardness, grain size, colour, how they hold water) that help us describe and compare samples.
materials: Optional: safe everyday objects for observation
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Test four soil/rock samples (touch, grain, water soak if allowed). Complete a property table and sort samples with a written rule. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: Sand drains fast / gritty; clay holds water / sticky — plants in sand may need more frequent water; clay can stay wetter. Reasoning: I used rock by attending to soil rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Calling all brown ground “dirt” without properties skips scientific description. Correction: Sand drains fast / gritty; clay holds water / sticky — plants in sand may need more frequent water; clay can stay wetter. Why: the correction restores accurate use of rock.

Parent: Likely misconception: Calling all brown ground “dirt” without properties skips scientific description. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Investigate or describe a fresh example (not the worked objects) that uses rock. Record evidence and explain how it supports your claim.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one science misconception about rock, correct it with evidence, and say why the correction works.

Parent: Marking notes: Require a new example, named observations and a claim–evidence link. / Require misconception + corrected claim + evidence reason..

WORKED MODEL

teach_steps.explain:
Rocks and soils have observable properties (hardness, grain size, colour, how they hold water) that help us describe and compare samples.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
